name: Dinka
confidence_why: Remijsen & Ladd (2008), Remijsen & Manyang (2009) and Blum (2023) all describe Rek-cluster Dinka as a language with four contrastive tonemes and no word-stress rule, Malou (1988) likewise finds phonemic tone and says any stress is non-contrastive with its conditioning unstudied, and the one competing 'stress' proposal, Gilley (2003), concerns vowel-quantity grades and was found acoustically unsupported in Luanyjang.

Dallas: SIL & University of Texas at Arlington (ERIC microfiche scan, archive.org). Paired with: Remijsen, Bert & Caguor Adong Manyang. 2009. Luanyjang Dinka. catalog_quote: Described in terms of the elements distributed in it and the features which characterize it, the phonological word is the unit of stress placement in the phonological hierarchy. Each phonological word has one and only one stress. The factors that condition stress have not been studied and, as mentioned, are not the concern of this discussion. It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection with semantic emphasis in Dinka. The final margin of the phonological word is characterized by potential pause. The phonological word is the level of distribution of the syllable: one syllable is stressed in each word. ... 2.3 The Syllable ... the syllable in Dinka is the unit of tone placement. Every syllable carries one and only one tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is a tone language (every syllable carries one tone, sec. 2.3; four tonemes per Remijsen & Ladd 2008 for Luanyjang) whose stems are almost all monosyllabic. Malou states that each phonological word (a unit bounded by potential pause, often host+clitic or a short phrase) bears exactly one non-contrastive stress, but explicitly declines to state what determines its position. His marked examples put the stress on the lexical head/root of the unit ('mony dit 'old man', 'ɣok lṳac 'pregnant cows', 'muoc meth 'give the child', but aca 'yat 'I have taken it' with stress on the verb root after the auxiliary clitic), i.e. consistent with root/head stress, though the author does not say so. The SW-specific modern descriptions (Remijsen & Manyang 2009: 120; Remijsen & Ladd 2008) give no stress rule at all: one toneme per morpheme, associated with the rightmost (usually only) syllable, with a predictable non-distinctive high pitch on the penult of disyllables; Gilley's (2003) 'stress' feature is a re-labelling of the morphological short vowel grade and found no acoustic support in Luanyjang (Remijsen & Gilley 2008, as reported in JIPA fn. 5).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Malou says the conditioning factors are unstudied. Remijsen & Manyang note polysyllables are limited to /aCVC/ nouns, loans and compounds.
new_statements.domain_note: Malou's domain is the 'phonological word' = pause-bounded unit larger than the grammatical word (his examples are two-word phrases and aux+verb groups); statement is for Dinka as a whole (four varieties incl. Western/Rek), from the author's own speech, variety not stated on the pages read. Citation-form monosyllables trivially carry the stress ('lec).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted stress statement (Malou 1988) is for Dinka as a whole (macro-language, glottocode dink1262), written by a native speaker whose own variety is not stated on the pages read; he lists 'Western, which is Rek based' among the four varieties his analysis is meant to cover. The Southwestern-specific modern descriptions are of Luanyjang (Luac) Dinka, Rek cluster, which Remijsen & Manyang 2009 place in South-Western Dinka = sout2832; those describe tone only and give no stress rule. Nebel 1948 (Rek-Malual, sout2832 proper) is silent on word stress. Remijsen 2013 (also saved) is Bor = Southeastern Dinka (sout2836) and should not be used for this key.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka is tonal (two level tones plus High-fall, Low-fall and Rise contours; tone carries grammatical and sg/pl contrasts). Words are largely monosyllabic CVC roots, so no syllable-placement rule for stress is given or possible; instead Gilley uses 'stress' for a paradigmatic, grammatically contrastive feature of the (monosyllabic) word: a 'stressed' word has its vowel shortened to about half the length of its unstressed counterpart, and stress vs. no stress (together with tone) distinguishes e.g. 2ps vs. 3ps readers on verbs (p. 5: 'Low tone plus stress indicates 2ps readers while Low tone without stress indicates 3ps readers') and singular vs. plural nouns (p. 10, tim/tiim). She notes that Andersen (1993) analyses the same facts as three degrees of vowel length and that 'stress' is her label for the extra-short/short and short/long steps. Examples are Rek dialect, stated to be representative of Rek, Bor, Agaar and Padang (p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: Underlyingly short root vowels cannot lengthen, so their stressed member is 'extra short' and the unstressed one 'just short' or 'lowered' (diphthongised, Duerksen 1989) (p. 10, ex. 43); in the proposed orthography it is the UNstressed word that is marked, with a word-final apostrophe (pp. 10-11); Andersen's (1993) three-length analysis is the competing account, 'a concept totally rejected by the Dinka themselves' (p. 10). In the Shilluk part, stress is marked orthographically by a straight or grave accent before the stressed syllable (p. 9), but that is Shilluk, not Dinka.
new_statements.identity_note: Gilley 2004's Dinka examples are explicitly Rek dialect (p. 4: 'Rek dialect is used in these examples, but is representative of all dialects: Rek, Bor, Agaar, and Padang'), i.e. Southwestern Dinka = sout2832; the conclusion mentions work 'with four dialects of Dinka'. The paper also treats Shilluk; the orthographic stress-accent-before-the-syllable convention (p. 9) is stated for Shilluk, not Dinka.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction among the sources opened, because the two readable works (Blum 2023; van Urk & Sun 2021) are silent on stress. The only stress statement on record remains Malou 1988 (one stress per phonological word, conditioning factors 'have not been studied', not contrastive), and the files already held by the project (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn. 5) plus Blum 2023 p. 8 cast doubt on Gilley's (2003) stress analysis (no acoustic support in Luanyjang; 'misleading' for ignoring tone). Tucker & Bryan 1966 and Gilley 2004 could not be opened, so whatever they say about stress is unverified. No disagreement about placement (no source gives a syllable-position rule; Dinka roots are monosyllabic). The sources differ on what 'stress' is: Malou 1988 (existing statement) treats it as a culminative property, one per phonological word with unstudied conditioning; Gilley 2004 (Rek data) treats 'stress' as a grammatically contrastive feature realised as vowel shortening ('about half its original length'), distinguishing e.g. 2ps vs 3ps readers and sg vs pl, and herself equates it with steps of Andersen's (1993) three-degree vowel-length contrast; the already-checked Remijsen & Manyang 2009 (fn. 5) reports that Gilley's 'stress' corresponds to the morphological short grade and that Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support for a separate stress feature in Luanyjang. So Gilley's 'stress' is best read as a length-grade label, not word stress in the metrical sense; all sources…

sources.citation: Remijsen, Bert & D. Robert Ladd. 2008. The tone system of the Luanyjang dialect of Dinka. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 29(2): 173-213. doi:10.1515/JALL.2008.009 (Edinburgh postprint via CORE)
sources.quote: Luanyjang Dinka has four tonemes (L, H, LH, HL), and each morpheme carries one, irrespective of its number of syllables. This toneme associates with the rightmost syllable, which is usually the only syllable. The internal composition or “weight” of the syllable is irrelevant to the association of tones. In utterances, the string of underlyingly specified tonemes is distorted due to the effect of tone sandhi processes. The most important of these is Dissimilatory Lowering, which turns H tone into L when it is preceded by H.
sources.locator: p. 207, sec. 4.1 Main findings (JALL 29(2)); methods p. 179-180, sec. 1.3; acoustic statistics p. 205-206, sec. 3
sources.note: No mention of word stress at all (the word 'stress/accent' appears only in reference titles). Sec. 2.3 and 4.1: four tonemes, one per morpheme regardless of syllable count, Association Rule links the toneme to the rightmost syllable of the morpheme; TBU = syllable; penult of /aCVC/ disyllables gets a predictable H.

Central to the approach advocated here is the combination of qualitative fieldwork data collection methods with instrumental analysis.' Expected to resta…

sources.note: From the abstract only: the article sorts Dinka noun singular/plural pairs by Andersen's vowel grades and nine tone classes and finds about half of the pairs synchronically regular, with the tonal alternation between the unmarked grade-1 form and the marked form falling mostly into three classes. It calls Luanyjang (Rek cluster) a four-tone dialect and Agar a three-tone dialect and reports the same tone classes valid across both; nothing on word stress and no acoustic measurement is mentioned in the abstract.

tone.quote: There are three contrasting tones: High /' /, Low / 'I, and Falling / ~ /, the latter falling from the level of High to the level of Low. The contrast is shown by the minimal triplets in (9)-(10). The superscript diacritics are used only once for each vowel, whatever the number of vowel symbols. … Tone is independent of vowel length (and of voice quality and vowel quality), except that the contrast between H and F seems to be neutralized on short vowels.
tone.locator: p.5-6, sec.2 'Phonological contrasts in monosyllabic words'; tone alternations sec.7 p.46-61
tone.summary: Three contrastive tones, High, Low and Falling (H-to-L fall), shown by minimal triplets; H vs Falling neutralized on short vowels; verb morphology marked by root, derivational and inflectional tones.
